summary: The retained run answered the residual I had named, and the answer closes the FSM-latency question rather than opening it. With the apply channel buffered so a caller can post without waiting, the backlog behind a 25ms FSM still stayed at zero entries and the main-loop probe came back at the idle baseline; with the channel unbuffered the backlog was one entry and the probe took three milliseconds against zero. Both declared comparisons held and are complete, so the blocked configuration I had flagged as the one where a queue could accumulate does not, in fact, accumulate one — delivery to the FSM is a single batch per commit and that send gates the main loop whether or not the client side is buffered. I recorded the interpretation with the honest boundary that the leak itself remains real and small (a few milliseconds per batch at a 25ms FSM) and that the magnitudes come from one delay, one cluster shape and one trial per configuration, while the separating evidence is the backlog operand rather than the probe latency. That is the last thing the run needed: every registered question is answered, and the final three answers were successful narrowings of my own earlier readings, each corrected by measurement — the source-only claim about FSM backpressure, the stronger stall phrasing, and now its named residual. The record closes holding three execution-grounded findings with their retained receipts, declared comparisons, witnesses and scoped conditions: the startup replay that blocks NewRaft once the committed-but-unapplied window exceeds the FSM channel's batch capacity, the nonvoter acknowledgement that satisfies VerifyLeader's voter quorum and can accompany committed state the confirming leader never applied, and the membership change that installs a voter immediately against two published descriptions that promise staging — alongside five suspicions refuted with evidence rather than argument, one behaviour entry corrected under its own id with its affected use answered, and no necessary gap outstanding.
